articles.title: A resume that works in seconds

body.support:
A **resume** shows an employer what you can do. Keep it to **one page**.

It has these parts, in order:

1. **Contact.** Name, phone, a sensible email.
2. **Profile.** Two lines about you and the job you want.
3. **Skills.** Like *teamwork* or *serving customers*.
4. **Experience.** Jobs, but also **sport**, **volunteering** and **school jobs**. Start each point with a doing word: *Served. Coached.*
5. **Education.** Your school and any certificates.
6. **References.** People who can say you're good. Ask them first.

Use clear headings. Check your spelling. You don't need a photo.
body.core:
A **resume** is a short document that shows an employer what you can do. For your first jobs, aim for **one page**.

Most resumes use the same **sections**, in this order:

1. **Contact details.** Name, phone, and an email that sounds grown-up (*first.last@*, not *partyking07@*).
2. **Profile.** Two lines: who you are and what work you're after.
3. **Skills.** Things like *customer service*, *teamwork*, *cash handling*. Only ones you can back up.
4. **Experience.** Jobs, but also **volunteering**, **sport**, **school leadership** and **helping in a family business**. Start each point with an **action verb**: *Served*, *Coached*, *Organised*.
5. **Education.** Your school, year level and any certificates (first aid, a VET course).
6. **References.** People who can vouch for you, like a coach or employer. Ask them first.

Then polish: **clear headings**, the same font and date style all the way through, and **no spelling mistakes**. In Australia you don't need a photo, your age or your date of birth.

Employers scan fast. Make the important things easy to spot.
body.extend:
A **resume** is a structured workplace document, and employers expect its conventions. For early-career roles, **one page** is standard.

The usual sections:

1. **Contact details**: name, phone and a professional email address.
2. **Profile**: a two-line summary of who you are and the work you're seeking, ideally tailored to the job.
3. **Key skills**: specific, honest and backed by evidence elsewhere on the page.
4. **Experience**: paid work, but also **volunteering**, **sport**, **leadership** and **family business**. Each point starts with an **action verb** and, where possible, a result: *Coached 12 under-10s; team made the finals.*
5. **Education and training**: school, year level, certificates (first aid, VET units).
6. **References**: people who have agreed to vouch for you, or “available on request”.

Presentation carries meaning: consistent headings, fonts and date formats signal care, and a single spelling error can signal the opposite. Australian resumes don't need a photo, age or date of birth.

Because recruiters scan quickly, design for the scan: headings and job titles should carry the key information on their own.

caseStudies.title: The seven-second scan

body.support:
A jobs website called **Ladders** studied how people read resumes. In **2018**, it found they spent about **7 seconds** on a first look.

Cameras tracked where their eyes went. They looked at **job titles** and **headings** first. Messy resumes turned them off.

Some experts say the study didn't share enough details. So 7 seconds isn't a rule.

But the big idea makes sense. Busy people **scan** first. Put your best stuff where they'll see it.
body.core:
**Ladders**, a US jobs website, studied how recruiters read resumes. In **2012** it reported that recruiters spent about **six seconds** on a first look. In **2018** it ran the study again: about **7.4 seconds**.

In the second study, recruiters were timed without knowing it. Then **eye-tracking** cameras showed where their eyes went. They looked at **job titles** and **headings** first. Messy layouts with no clear headings turned them off.

Some experts say the study left out important details, like how many recruiters took part and what jobs they were hiring for. So **7.4 seconds** isn't a rule.

But the main idea makes sense: busy people **scan** first. If your best stuff is buried, they might never see it.
body.extend:
**Ladders**, a US careers site, published widely shared research on how recruiters read resumes. Its **2012** study reported an initial screen of about **six seconds**; a **2018** follow-up reported about **7.4 seconds**.

The 2018 study had two stages: recruiters were timed, without knowing it, as they sorted a stack of resumes, and then **eye-tracking** recorded where they looked in a lab. They focused on **job titles** and **headings**, and were put off by layouts without clear sections or with text that didn't draw the eye down the page.

Critics point out that the published report leaves out key details, such as how many recruiters took part, their experience, and the kinds of roles involved. Some see it as partly a marketing piece. So the exact figure shouldn't be treated as fact.

Still, the core finding fits common sense and other advice: first reads are fast and selective. A resume should be designed for the scan.

teacher.overview: Students learn the requirements and conventions of a resume (sections, scannable layout, action verbs, consistency, accuracy), turn their real experience into skills, decode workplace jargon, and build and test their own one-page resume. The case study is the Ladders eye-tracking study (about 7 seconds), including criticism of its method.
prep: Have a resume template ready (Youth Central has Victorian ones; your school may have its own).
Optional: a local employer or careers adviser to give feedback.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — What goes in
steps: **Hook (10 min):** the 7-second test on two sample resumes. What did you remember?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** six sections; action verbs.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Make it sound like you
steps: **Rewrite (15 min):** make it sound like a skill.
**Case study (15 min):** the seven-second scan; discuss trusting statistics.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Build it, test it
steps: **Hands-on (30 min):** build the resume, 7-second test, feedback.
**Level Up (10 min):** tailor to a real ad.

teacher.answers:
**Resume:** 1 contact details; 2 profile; 3 skills; 4 experience (action verbs, volunteering counts); 5 education and certificates; 6 references.

**Keep or cut:** party email — cut; football captain — keep; beach photo — cut; first aid — keep; sleeping/scrolling — cut; family takeaway — keep.

**Jargon:** casual = paid by the hour, no guaranteed hours, higher hourly rate (casual loading); availability = days/times you can work; RSA = Responsible Service of Alcohol (a certificate needed to serve alcohol); proficient = skilled, competent.

realityCheck: **“I've got nothing to put on it.”** You'll hear this a lot. Spend real time on the gathering step: sport, caring for siblings, family business, gaming communities, school jobs. Everyone has something.
**Personal details stay private.** Students will type real phone numbers and addresses. Remind them not to post resumes publicly; suburb only, not a full street address, is fine.
**Some students carry heavy responsibilities** (carers, working in a family business). Treat these as the strengths they are.
**Device time is the bottleneck.** Formatting eats time. Use a template so lesson 3 is about content and testing, not fonts.
**Works in a real class:** absolutely. Students leave with a real document they can use this week, which is the most motivating outcome in the set. It pairs well with Job Hunt and Apply for Real.

levels.support: Aimed at about Year 5 reading: simpler article and case study, 6 key words, 3-choice quiz, word bank, fewer sort cards and rows, and a fill-in template.
levels.core: Aimed at about Year 7 reading: the standard version with annotation, keep or cut, skill rewrites, jargon, the case study and building a real resume.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 9 reading: richer conventions, judging the study's evidence, tailoring to a real job ad, and adult feedback.
